subject: chemistry
title: Elephant toothpaste: a catalyst at work

steps.title: Put on goggles
steps.instruction: Hydrogen peroxide irritates skin and eyes and the foam comes out hot. Goggles on (and gloves in a real lab).

whatIf.no_ppe: A single splash in an unprotected eye can cause lasting damage, which is why goggles go on before any bottle is opened.

steps.title: 20 mL hydrogen peroxide
steps.instruction: Pour 20 mL of 6% hydrogen peroxide into the measuring cylinder. It stands in a tray to catch the foam.

whatIf.too_fast: Fast pouring splashes peroxide, which bleaches and stings skin.
whatIf.wrong_amount: More peroxide makes a bigger, hotter foam that can overflow the tray.

steps.title: 5 drops of washing-up liquid
steps.instruction: Add about 5 drops of washing-up liquid. It will trap the gas as bubbles.

whatIf.wrong_order: Without detergent already in, the gas just escapes and you see fizzing, not foam.

steps.title: Light the Bunsen
steps.instruction: Light the Bunsen burner: you need a glowing splint ready before the catalyst goes in.

steps.title: Light a splint
steps.instruction: Hold the wooden splint in the flame until it catches.

steps.title: Blow it out so it glows
steps.instruction: Blow the flame out. The tip should keep glowing red: this is a glowing splint.

steps.title: Add the catalyst
steps.instruction: Pour in 5 mL of potassium iodide solution in one go, then step back.

whatIf.no_ppe: The foam is hot and contains peroxide and iodine, which stain and irritate skin and eyes.
whatIf.wrong_amount: More catalyst only makes the foam come faster: the catalyst is not used up, so it does not make more oxygen.

steps.title: Watch the foam
steps.instruction: Watch the foam surge out of the cylinder. Feel how warm the cylinder is (the temperature readout).

steps.title: Test the gas
steps.instruction: Hold the glowing splint at the mouth of the cylinder, just above the foam.

whatIf.wrong_order: A splint that is still burning just burns a bit brighter; only a glowing splint relighting is a clear test for oxygen.

safe-2.text: Pick up the goggles and put them on before you touch any bottle.

vol-2.text: Pick up the peroxide bottle and pour 20 mL into the cylinder.

soap-1.text: Something has to trap the gas in bubbles.

soap-2.text: Add drops from the washing-up liquid bottle to the cylinder.

burn-1.text: You need a flame to light the splint.

burn-2.text: Light the Bunsen, then hold the splint in the flame.

burn-3.text: Watch the burner light and the splint catch.

glow-1.text: The oxygen test uses a splint that glows, not one that burns.

glow-2.text: With the lit splint in your hand, choose Blow out.

glow-3.text: Watch the flame go out and the tip glow.

cat-1.text: Peroxide breaks down very slowly on its own. What speeds it up?

cat-2.text: Pour 5 mL of potassium iodide into the cylinder.

foam-2.text: Watch the cylinder: the foam rises out of the top.

test-1.text: Which gas relights a glowing splint?

test-2.text: Pick up the glowing splint and choose To tube mouth, then the cylinder.

observations.whatHappened: As soon as the potassium iodide went in, a column of warm foam shot up out of the cylinder. A glowing splint held in the gas burst back into flame.
observations.why: Hydrogen peroxide slowly breaks down into water and oxygen. Iodide ions are a catalyst: they give the reaction an easier route (lower activation energy), so it happens thousands of times faster, and they are not used up. The washing-up liquid traps the oxygen in millions of bubbles, making foam. The reaction gives out heat, so the foam is warm. Oxygen relights a glowing splint because it helps things burn.
realWorld: Catalase in your liver breaks down peroxide the same way
Peroxide as a bleach and disinfectant

prompts.question: The glowing splint relit. Which gas was made?
prompts.explain: Oxygen relights a glowing splint. Hydrogen gives a squeaky pop instead.

prompts.question: What did the potassium iodide do?
choices: It reacted and was used up
It acted as a catalyst, speeding up the breakdown without being used up
prompts.explain: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by lowering the activation energy and is left over at the end.

prompts.question: The cylinder got warm. The reaction is...
prompts.explain: It releases energy to the surroundings, so it is exothermic.

captions.text: Goggles on. Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is slowly falling apart into water and oxygen all the time.
A few drops of washing-up liquid will trap any gas as bubbles.
Get a glowing splint ready: it is the test for oxygen.
Now the catalyst: iodide ions give the breakdown a much easier route, so it speeds up enormously.
Oxygen + soap = a column of foam. It's warm too: the reaction is exothermic.
The glowing splint relights: the gas is oxygen. The catalyst is not used up.
